title: The Librarian Who Saved Islamic Philosophy
event_summary: When the Almohad caliph al-Ma'mun reversed his dynasty's official endorsement of Ibn Tumart's rigid theological doctrines, a quiet purge of rationalist philosophical texts was already well underway across North Africa. A court librarian named Ibn al-Qattan al-Marrakushi, working in the royal library of Marrakesh, systematically copied and smuggled key manuscripts of Ibn Rushd (Averroes) — including his comprehensive commentaries on Aristotle — to Jewish scholars and merchants with connections to Provence and Sicily. Without these rescued copies, which were translated into Latin by scholars like Michael Scot at Frederick II's court, the Aristotelian revival that transformed European thought from Thomas Aquinas onward would have lacked its primary textual foundation.
why_forgotten: The Almohad regime had political reasons to erase both Ibn Rushd's legacy and anyone who defied their ideological control over knowledge. European scholars who received the translations preferred to credit the Greek originals rather than acknowledge their dependence on Muslim intermediaries. Ibn al-Qattan himself left few records, and his role was subsumed into broader narratives of anonymous 'transmission' between civilizations.
why_it_matters: The Aristotelian commentaries of Ibn Rushd, preserved through this chain, became the intellectual engine of European scholasticism, directly shaping the university curriculum that still structures Western higher education. The concept of the 'double truth' — that reason and faith could operate independently — which Aquinas wrestled with and the Latin Averroists championed, laid groundwork for the eventual separation of science from theology. Every modern university department that treats philosophy and theology as distinct disciplines owes an unacknowledged debt to a Moroccan librarian's defiance.
